verdict.rationale: The canon places restrictive diction (didaskein de gynaiki ouk epitrepo oude authentein andros in 1 Tim 2:12, sigatosan and hypotassesthosan in 1 Cor 14:34) beside the male-marked office qualifications (mias gynaikos andra in 1 Tim 3:2 and Titus 1:6) and over against texts of mutual standing and female ministry (Gal 3:28, Phoibe diakonos in Rom 16:1, and the name Iounian in Rom 16:7). The verdict turns on lemmas whose sense the words do not settle. A direct query confirms authenteo (G0831) is a hapax occurring only at 1 Tim 2:12, and the lexicon itself records both a neutral sense, to have full power or authority over, and a pejorative sense, to domineer, with no second canonical use to fix which is meant. The present epitrepo (G2010), I do not permit, is the same verb used elsewhere for granting permission to speak in a particular setting, and sigao (G4601) appears three times in 1 Cor 14 (verses 28, 30, 34), the first two governing specific disorders, so the scope of the women command is contestable between an absolute prohibition and a setting-bound one. The office noun episkopos is grammatically masculine and the mias gynaikos andra clause presupposes a married male on its surface, yet that clause can be read as a fidelity standard, and the 1 Cor 14:34-35 unit carries a known transposition the ingested apparatus cannot adjudicate. Because the same lemmas yield more than one grammatically defensible reading, the lexical pattern is contested rather than decisive.

scripture.force: didaskein de gynaiki ouk epitrepo oude authentein andros, all einai en hesychia, I do not permit a woman to teach or to authentein over a man, but to be in quietness. Two infinitives, didaskein, to teach, and authentein, the verb in question, are joined by oude. A direct query confirms authenteo occurs nowhere else in the canon, so it is a hapax, and the lexicon records it with both a neutral sense, to have full power or authority over, and a pejorative sense, to domineer, leaving the canon with no second use to fix the force. epitrepo is a first person present, I do not permit, and the same verb is used elsewhere for granting permission to speak in a particular instance, so it is debated whether it states a standing rule or a directive in a situation. The two infinitives can be read as two separate prohibitions or as one composite idea, to teach in a domineering manner, and the morphology does not decide between them.

Adam gar protos eplasthe, eita Eua, for Adam was formed first, then Eve. The gar introduces a ground for the preceding directive, and the appeal to the order of formation pulls the prohibition toward a trans-cultural basis rather than a purely local one. A query confirms both Adam and Eua are present in the verse. Whether the order-of-formation argument grounds a permanent office restriction or supports a contextual correction is not fixed by the conjunction alone, since gar marks explanation without specifying the scope of what it explains.

dei oun ton episkopon anepilempton einai, mias gynaikos andra, the overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife. A query confirms episkopos occurs seven times in the canon and is grammatically masculine here, and the qualification mias gynaikos andra, a one-woman man, presupposes a male officeholder in its plain construction. Yet the clause can be read as a character standard for marital fidelity rather than a bare sex requirement, and grammatical masculine gender for an office term does not by itself exclude a female referent, since masculine forms serve as the default for mixed or generic reference in Greek.

ei tis estin anenklethos, mias gynaikos aner, if anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife, set in the context of appointing presbyterous, elders, in every town. The same mias gynaikos aner formula recurs, again presupposing a married male in its surface sense. The opening tis, anyone, is the indefinite pronoun and is not itself sex-marked, so the restriction to men rests on the gynaikos aner phrase rather than on tis, and that phrase is read by some as a fidelity qualification rather than a sex bar.

hai gynaikes en tais ekklesiais sigatosan, the women are to keep silent in the assemblies, ou gar epitrepetai autais lalein, alla hypotassesthosan, for they are not permitted to speak, but to be in submission. A query confirms sigao appears three times in this one chapter, at verses 28, 30, and 34, where a tongue-speaker is to sigato if there is no interpreter and a prophet is to sigato when another receives a revelation. The proximity of three sigao commands, each governing a specific disorder, makes the scope of the women command contestable between an absolute prohibition and a setting-bound regulation of disruptive speech.

ouk eni arsen kai thely, there is no male and female, pantes gar hymeis heis este en Christo Iesou, for you are all one in Christ Jesus. A query confirms the two sex nouns arsen, male, and thely, female, are both present, joined to eni, there is, and heis, one. Whether this negation of the male-and-female distinction speaks only to justification and inheritance, the immediate argument about heirship and being Abraham's seed, or extends to ministry roles is not settled by the lexemes, since the context is sonship rather than church office, yet the comprehensiveness of pantes heis pulls against any sex-based exclusion.

synistemi de hymin Phoiben ten adelphen hemon, ousan diakonon tes ekklesias, I commend to you Phoebe our sister, who is a diakonos of the church. A query confirms the noun diakonos is applied to the named woman Phoebe in connection with a specific congregation, and that diakonos occurs in twenty-eight verses ranging from general servant to a recognized function. Because the term spans that range across the canon, it complicates a blanket exclusion of women from recognized service, though it does not by itself establish that Phoebe held the overseeing or teaching office named in the qualification lists.

aspasasthe Andronikon kai Iounian, greet Andronicus and Junia, hoitines eisin episemoi en tois apostolois, who are episemoi en tois apostolois. A query shows the lexical store records the accusative name Iounian under one Strong number with both a feminine lemma form, Iounia, Junia, and a masculine lemma form, Iounias, Junias, so the sex of the person is itself a lexical open question. The verse also contains episemos, notable, and apostolos. The phrase en tois apostolois can mean among the apostles, marking the pair as apostles, or well known to the apostles, marking them as esteemed by the apostles. If Junia is feminine and the inclusive sense holds, a woman is numbered among a class of apostoloi, which complicates a strict office restriction.

complicating_texts.resolution: The phrase ouk eni arsen kai thely, no male and female, negates the sex distinction within standing in Christ and complicates any sex-based office bar. It is addressed by observing that the surrounding argument concerns justification, sonship, and being Abraham's seed and heirs, not the appointment of overseers, so the lexemes establish equal standing without by themselves extending to or excluding office. A query confirms both sex nouns arsen and thely are present. The text is genuinely two-edged, which contributes to the disputed verdict rather than resolving it.

Phoebe is called diakonos of the church at Cenchreae, applying a ministry term to a named woman and complicating a blanket exclusion. A query confirms diakonos here and shows the noun ranges across twenty-eight verses from general servant to a designated function, so the title does not by itself prove she held the overseeing or teaching office that the qualification lists describe. The term pulls toward female ministry without settling whether the disputed office was open to women.

Two intertwined lexical questions remain unresolved on the queried data. The store records the accusative Iounian under one Strong number with both a feminine lemma, Iounia, and a masculine lemma, Iounias, so the sex of the person is genuinely open in the lexical layer, and the prepositional phrase en tois apostolois is ambiguous between inclusive among the apostles and comparative well known to the apostles. The ingested data carries the variant name forms but no accentual or contextual datum that closes either question, so it is left unaddressed and flagged as a complicating text the lexical store could not resolve.

The silence command carries a known transposition in the manuscript tradition, where some witnesses place verses 34-35 after verse 40. A direct query of the variant store shows it holds variant units for 3 John only, so this passage falls outside the ingested apparatus and the location and originality question cannot be examined here. Because the placement bears on how absolutely the command should be read, the matter is left unresolved and flagged, and it is part of why the verdict is recorded as variant-sensitive.

variants.note: A direct query of the ingested variant store confirms VariantUnit data is present for 3 John only, so no apparatus layer covers 1 Corinthians 14 or 1 Timothy 2. The cited 1 Corinthians 14:34-35 unit is well known to carry a transposition in part of the tradition, where the verses appear after verse 40, and the originality and placement of the silence command bear directly on how absolutely it should be read, so the verdict is marked variant-sensitive. These books fall outside the published CBGM scope, which covers 3 John, so the status is recorded as ecm-shadow.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads ouk epitrepo in 1 Tim 2:12 as a standing rule expressed in the present tense, takes the two infinitives didaskein and authentein as distinct prohibited acts, teaching and exercising authority, and reads the hapax authenteo in its neutral lexicon sense of holding authority over. It grounds the rule trans-culturally on the creation-order gar of 1 Tim 2:13, Adam formed first, and treats the male-marked mias gynaikos andra of 1 Tim 3:2 and Titus 1:6, together with the masculine episkopos, as defining a male officeholder. It reads Gal 3:28 as equal standing in Christ rather than role, and reads Phoebe's diakonos and the Romans 16:7 phrase as not establishing the overseeing or teaching office for women, taking en tois apostolois as well known to the apostles.

Reads the hapax authenteo in its pejorative lexicon sense, to domineer or usurp, so the prohibition targets domineering rather than ordinary authority, and notes there is no second canonical use to settle the sense. It takes the present epitrepo and the situational vocabulary as addressing a particular disorder, and reads the 1 Cor 14:34 sigao alongside the chapter's two other situational silencings in verses 28 and 30. It takes mias gynaikos andra as a fidelity qualification rather than a sex bar, reads Gal 3:28 as comprehensive of male and female, and takes Phoebe diakonos and a feminine Junia counted among the apostles as evidence that recognized ministry, including authoritative roles, was open to women.

Reads the restrictive texts as one point within a trajectory whose direction, traced from the equal-standing language of Gal 3:28 and the female ministry references, points beyond the first-century application, so that the lexemes describe an apostolic instruction whose permanence is itself the contested question rather than a datum the words settle. On this reading the vocabulary fixes what was said but not how far it reaches in time.

hermeneutics.notes: All three lenses operate on the same anchor lemmas and reach different conclusions by assigning the hapax authenteo either its neutral or its pejorative lexicon sense, by reading the present epitrepo and sigao as either standing or situational, by construing the grammatical masculine of the office nouns and the mias gynaikos andra clause as either sex-restrictive or character-descriptive, and by deciding the referential reach of Gal 3:28 and the sex and standing of Junia. The disagreement is over the sense and scope of contested lexemes, not over agreed morphology, which is why the lexical pattern is contested rather than decisive. Both lens senses for authenteo are attested in the queried lexicon, so neither reading can be excluded on lexical grounds alone.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Determine whether the canonical lexical pattern reserves the overseeing and teaching office to qualified men, examining the restrictive diction of 1 Tim 2:12 and 1 Cor 14:34, the male-marked office qualifications of 1 Tim 3:2 and Titus 1:6, and the texts of mutual standing and female ministry such as Gal 3:28, Rom 16:1, and Rom 16:7, without presupposing which set of texts controls.
stem_audit.notes: The stem phrases the proposition as a denial that women are to hold the eldership or teaching-pastor office over mixed adult assemblies, which already encodes a particular harmonization of the restrictive and the inclusive texts and labels one office configuration as the norm. The categories teaching-pastor office and mixed adult assemblies are not themselves lexemes in the cited texts, so the stem imports a polity framework the words do not supply. The verdict is derived on the original stem, and the audit records that direct queries confirm the lexicon furnishes neither a settled sense for the hapax authenteo nor a term that fixes the scope of didaskein or sigao.

lay_summary: The question asks whether the Bible reserves the elder and overseer office, and the teaching role over mixed adult gatherings, to qualified men. The Greek words in the cited verses point in two directions, and that is the heart of the dispute. Some verses sound restrictive. First Timothy 2:12 says I do not permit a woman to teach, didaskein, or to authentein over a man. A direct search of the text confirms the verb authenteo appears only here in the whole New Testament, so there is no other passage to fix its sense, and the lexicon lists it with two meanings at once, to hold authority over and to domineer. The word permit, epitrepo, is in the present tense and is the same verb used elsewhere for letting someone speak on a given occasion, so readers differ on whether it states a permanent rule or a situational one. First Corinthians 14:34 says the women should keep silent, sigao, in the assemblies, and the same word is used twice nearby, in verses 28 and 30, for a tongue-speaker and a prophet who should fall silent in specific cases, which raises the question whether the women command is absolute or aimed at a particular disorder. The office lists in 1 Timothy 3:2 and Titus 1:6 say the overseer should be a one-woman man, mias gynaikos andra, which on its face pictures a married man, though some read this as a faithfulness standard rather than a rule barring women. Other verses point the opposite way. Galatians 3:28 says there is no male and female, you are all one in Christ, though its argument is about standing and inheritance. Romans 16:1 calls Phoebe a diakonos, a servant or minister, of her church, a term that ranges from general service to a recognized role. Romans 16:7 greets Junia as notable among the apostles, and the lexical data carries her name in both a feminine and a masculine form, so even the sex of the person is unsettled, and the Greek phrase can mean among the apostles or well known to the apostles. The trouble is that the words themselves do not settle these questions. A single rare verb with two attested senses, a silence command that may be situational, an office phrase that may describe character, and a name that may or may not be feminine all leave room for more than one careful reading. Because the same vocabulary supports both a restrictive and an inclusive conclusion, and because the silence text also carries a known manuscript question about where it belongs, the lexical pattern here is genuinely contested rather than decisive.
